analysis.one_liner: Bars class action lawsuits alleging companies misclassified employees as independent contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote, having drawn no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the federal rules governing class actions to prevent a lawsuit from even being certified if its core claim is that a company wrongly labeled its workers as independent contractors. Companies in the gig economy — ride-hail, delivery, and similar contractor-based businesses — are the most common defendants in such misclassification suits, which workers bring to win wages, overtime, and benefits denied to people classified as contractors. The bill would have taken away that group route, forcing workers to sue one at a time.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that rely on classifying their workers as independent contractors, especially gig-economy platforms. Misclassification class actions are the main legal tool gig workers use to recover unpaid wages, expenses, and benefits, and they can cost companies large settlements. Blocking them removes that exposure and locks in the contractor model.

how_it_helps.text: Amends Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure so a class action cannot be certified if the claim alleges employees were misclassified as independent contractors [S3].
The stated purpose is to protect the gig economy and small businesses that operate through contractor services from costly class action litigation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers classified as independent contractors — gig drivers, delivery workers, and other contractor labor — who would lose the practical ability to bring group claims for wages and benefits. Filing one at a time is usually not worth it for small individual claims, which is exactly why misclassification cases are brought as class actions.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating misclassification class actions removes workers' main enforcement path: most misclassification damages per worker are too small to justify an individual lawsuit, so the claims would effectively vanish rather than move to individual courts [S2,S3].

The bill changes federal court rules to settle a contested labor-law question by litigation rule rather than by legislation or rulemaking, bypassing the normal process for amending the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure through the Judicial Conference [S3].

It would shield not only gig platforms but any employer accused of misclassification, including those that misclassify to avoid payroll taxes, overtime, and benefits, shifting those costs onto workers and public programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes to one side: companies that depend on the contractor model would avoid potentially large settlements and gain certainty, while the workers whose claims it targets would lose their only realistic route to court. There is no provision compensating misclassified workers another way.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, then sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, the first day of the 117th Congress [S1,S5].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on January 4, 2021 [S5].
On March 1, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors and never advanced past the subcommittee referral [S4,S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig workers and their ability to use class actions are better off; the contractor-based businesses the bill would have shielded gained nothing because it never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gig workers, whose lawsuits stayed available

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood [S4].

industries.note: These are the most frequent defendants in misclassification class actions, so the bill would have lifted a major litigation threat and secured the contractor model they depend on. It never advanced, so nothing changed for them.

industries.industry: Other businesses that rely on independent-contractor labor
industries.note: The bill's protection was written broadly for any employer facing a misclassification class action, not just gig companies. Workers would have borne the cost through lost wage claims.
